title: LG releases K-EXAONE 2.0, a 750-billion-parameter open-source model, on Hugging Face
subtitle: South Korea's largest frontier model ships under Apache 2.0 with 37B active parameters, a 262,144-token context window, and benchmark scores that put it within reach of GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5 on reasoning and code.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: LG AI Research published K-EXAONE 2.0 on Hugging Face on July 31, releasing what it calls the largest frontier AI model ever built in South Korea. The architecture is a 750-billion-parameter mixture of experts with 37 billion active parameters, 256 experts of which 8 are activated per token, and a 262,144-token context window. Coverage spans 10 languages, including Korean, English, Japanese, and Chinese. LG shipped FP8 and NVFP4 quantizations alongside the base weights and supports speculative decoding — MTP and DSpark — for a claimed 3–5x inference speedup. The license is Apache 2.0, which permits commercial use without restriction.

The benchmark scores put the model in serious company. K-EXAONE 2.0 posts 83.5 on MMLU-Pro, 92.3 on AIME 2026, 68.2 on SWE-Bench Verified, and 94.4 on OpenAI-MRCR. Those numbers do not top the US frontier — Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol are still ahead on most — but they are close enough that for many enterprise workloads the choice will come down to cost, latency, and license. Under Apache 2.0, an enterprise can host K-EXAONE 2.0 on its own hardware, fine-tune it on proprietary data, and ship the result in a product without paying LG a cent. That is a different economic surface than an OpenAI or Anthropic API integration.

In the broader context, this is the third major open-weight release from Asia in six weeks: Moonshot's Kimi K3 (2.8T parameters, July 17), Thinking Machines' Inkling (975B, July 16), and now K-EXAONE 2.0. Together they represent something that did not exist at the start of 2026 — a working alternative frontier stack that is not licensed from a US lab. For South Korea specifically, this is also a sovereignty story: LG describes the release as a deliberate response to the risk that Korean data, Korean language use, and Korean industrial workflows would end up dependent on models trained and hosted overseas.

For learners: the practical significance of the Apache 2.0 license is worth understanding. It means you can download K-EXAONE 2.0 tonight, run it on your own GPUs (or on a cloud provider of your choice), and build a product on top without asking permission. If you are a student in Korea, Japan, or Southeast Asia and your work involves those languages, this may be the first frontier-class model you can actually train against your local data at reasonable cost. Try the FP8 quantization first — the memory footprint is roughly a quarter of the full-precision weights and the quality loss is small.
